title: Charts, graphs, maps, diagrams and other visuals
blurb: Read the title, axes, units, legend and scale first, then interpret and apply bar, line and pie charts, flowcharts, maps and org charts.
question: A bar graph is titled 'Clinic visits by month (in hundreds)', and February's bar reaches 8. One answer choice says 8 visits and another says 800. Which is right, and what part of the graph decides it?

teach.h: Read the frame before the data
teach.body: Formally, analyzing a visual means identifying its title, axes and units, scale, legend or key, labels and source, then interpreting the data (largest, smallest, change, trend, share of a whole) and applying it to a situation. In plain English: before you look at a single bar, read the frame around it. The frame tells you what is being measured and in what units, and most wrong answers come from skipping it.

items: Title: what is shown, for whom, and when?
Axes and units: what does each axis measure? Watch for 'in hundreds', 'in thousands', percent or count.
Legend or key: which color, pattern or line is which series?
Scale: how much is each gridline, inch or symbol worth?
Now read the question and find only the data it asks about. Do not go beyond the visual.

teach.caption: The title's '(in hundreds)' multiplies every bar by 100. Reading the bar height alone gives an answer 100 times too small.
Use the legend: Clinic A (solid) rises every week; Clinic B (dashed) falls. They cross between weeks 2 and 3.

teach.body: A pie chart shows each part as a share of one whole, usually in percent. To turn a share into a number of people, multiply by the total: if 20% of 200 surveyed students walk to class, 0.20 × 200 = 40 students walk. A slice that looks bigger is a bigger share of THIS whole only; two pie charts with different totals cannot be compared slice by slice without the totals.

Best at showing
Typical question
rows: When did it rise or fall?
teach.caption: Also expect maps (legend, compass rose, scale), diagrams with labeled parts, timelines, org charts and floor plans.

children.label: Take it to the front desk
Return bin, then pay at kiosk

teach.caption: Follow the arrows from the start, answering each decision for the case in the question.
Map distance × scale = real distance: 2.5 inches × 25 miles = 62.5 miles.

teach.text: Visual traps: ignoring 'in hundreds' or 'in thousands'; reading the wrong series from the legend; extending a trend past the last data point ('it will reach...'); treating a percent as a count; following a flowchart branch that does not fit the case; and applying a map scale backward (dividing instead of multiplying).

teach.body: Tanya Wilson, applying to a radiography program, sees the clinic-visits graph and is asked how many visits there were in February. The bar reaches 8, and '8' is the first option. She rereads the title, spots '(in hundreds)', and answers 800. Asked whether visits will top 1,000 in May, she notes the graph ends in April: nothing in it supports a May figure.

items: Read the title, axes, units, legend and scale before any data.
Bar = compare amounts; line = change over time; pie = parts of a whole; flowchart = steps and decisions.
Percent × total = count. A share is not a number of people.
Follow flowchart arrows and decisions for the exact case; multiply map distance by the scale.
Stay inside the visual: do not predict beyond its last data point.

summary: You can now read charts, graphs, flowcharts, maps and org charts by checking the title, units, legend and scale first. You can then interpret and apply the data without falling for unit, series, percent-versus-count or extrapolation traps.

A.q:
A bar graph is titled 'Visits to Pine Clinic, by month (in hundreds)'. The bars show: January 6, February 8, March 5, April 9.

According to the graph, how many visits did the clinic have in February?
A.why: The title says the values are in hundreds, so a bar of 8 means 8 × 100 = 800 visits.

whyNot.0: This reads the bar height and ignores '(in hundreds)' in the title.
whyNot.3: This treats the units as thousands instead of hundreds.

A.q:
A line graph shows patients seen per week at two clinics. Legend: solid line = Clinic A, dashed line = Clinic B.
Week 1: A 40, B 55
Week 2: A 48, B 50
Week 3: A 60, B 45
Week 4: A 66, B 42

Which statement is supported by the graph?
options: Clinic B saw more patients than Clinic A in every week
Clinic B's weekly count rose steadily over the 4 weeks
The two clinics saw the same number of patients in Week 2
Clinic A's weekly count went up in each week shown
A.why: Clinic A went from 40 to 48 to 60 to 66: an increase every week.

whyNot.0: Clinic B saw more only in Weeks 1 and 2; Clinic A saw more in Weeks 3 and 4.
whyNot.1: This describes Clinic A's line. Clinic B fell from 55 to 42.
whyNot.2: In Week 2, Clinic A saw 48 and Clinic B saw 50: close, but not the same.

A.q:
A pie chart shows how 200 surveyed nursing students get to campus: car 45%, bus 25%, walk 20%, bike 10%.

How many of the surveyed students walk to campus?

whyNot.0: This treats the percent as a count; 20% is a share, not 20 people.
whyNot.2: 45 is the car percentage, a different slice.
whyNot.3: 50 students is the bus slice (25% of 200).

B.q:
A flowchart for returning library books reads:
Start: Is the book damaged?
  Yes: Take it to the front desk.
  No: Is it overdue?
     Yes: Put it in the return bin, then pay the fine at the kiosk.
     No: Put it in the return bin.

Ana's book is undamaged but three days overdue. According to the flowchart, what should she do?
options: Put it in the bin, then pay the fine
Take it to the front desk for staff
Put it in the return bin and leave
Pay at the kiosk, then go to the desk
B.why: Not damaged sends Ana down the 'No' branch to 'Is it overdue?'. It is overdue, so she follows 'Yes': return bin, then pay at the kiosk.

whyNot.1: The front desk is the branch for damaged books.
whyNot.2: This is the branch for books that are not overdue.
whyNot.3: No branch sends an undamaged book to the front desk.

B.q:
On a campus map, the scale bar shows 1 inch = 400 feet. On the map, the library is 2.5 inches from the student center.

About how far apart are the two buildings?
options: 160 feet
400 feet
1,000 feet
10,000 feet
B.why: Multiply map distance by the scale: 2.5 × 400 feet = 1,000 feet.

whyNot.0: This divides 400 by 2.5 instead of multiplying.
whyNot.1: 400 feet is the distance for 1 inch, not 2.5 inches.

B.q:
A table shows average weekly attendance at a farmers market: June 220, July 260, August 300.

Which statement is best supported by the table?
options: Attendance doubled between June and August
Attendance rose by 40 people each month shown
Attendance will reach 340 people in September
Attendance was highest in the month of July
B.why: 220 to 260 is an increase of 40, and 260 to 300 is another 40.

whyNot.2: The table ends in August. A September figure extends the trend beyond the data.

C.q:
A dosing chart for a children's liquid medicine shows:
24-35 lb: 5 mL
36-47 lb: 7.5 mL
48-59 lb: 10 mL
60-71 lb: 12.5 mL

A child weighed 47 lb last month and weighs 49 lb now. According to the chart, how does the child's dose change?
options: It increases by 2.5 mL
It stays the same
It increases by 5 mL
It decreases by 2.5 mL
C.why: At 47 lb the child was in the 36-47 lb row (7.5 mL). At 49 lb the child is in the 48-59 lb row (10 mL). 10 − 7.5 = an increase of 2.5 mL.

whyNot.1: 47 lb and 49 lb fall in different rows, so the dose changes.
whyNot.2: This jumps two rows (to 12.5 mL); 49 lb is in the 48-59 lb row.
whyNot.3: The heavier weight is in a higher-dose row, so the dose rises.

C.q:
A bar graph titled 'Average hours of sleep per night, by year in a nursing program' shows: Year 1, 7.2; Year 2, 6.8; Year 3, 6.1; Year 4, 6.5.

Which statement is supported by the graph?
options: Year 3 students had the lowest average sleep
Average sleep fell in each year of the program
Year 4 students slept more than Year 1 students
Sleep fell by over an hour from Year 1 to Year 2
C.why: Year 3's bar (6.1 hours) is the lowest of the four.

whyNot.1: Sleep rose from Year 3 (6.1) to Year 4 (6.5).
whyNot.2: Year 4 averaged 6.5 hours, less than Year 1's 7.2.
whyNot.3: From 7.2 to 6.8 is a drop of 0.4 hours, under half an hour.

C.q:
An organizational chart shows: the Chief Nursing Officer oversees the Director of Inpatient Care and the Director of Outpatient Care. The Nurse Managers of 3 West and 4 East report to the Director of Inpatient Care. The Nurse Manager of the Day Surgery Center reports to the Director of Outpatient Care.

To whom does the Nurse Manager of 4 East report directly?
options: The Chief Nursing Officer
The Director of Outpatient Care
The Nurse Manager of 3 West
The Director of Inpatient Care
C.why: The chart places the 4 East Nurse Manager directly under the Director of Inpatient Care.

whyNot.0: The Chief Nursing Officer is two levels up; the Director sits between them.
whyNot.1: The Director of Outpatient Care oversees the Day Surgery Center, a different branch.
whyNot.2: The 3 West Nurse Manager is a peer at the same level, not a supervisor.

reteach.title: A recipe card has a frame too
reteach.question: A recipe says '2 c. flour, serves 4'. You are cooking for 8. What do you have to read besides the number 2 before you start?

blocks.body: '2' means nothing until you see 'c.' (cups, not tablespoons) and 'serves 4' (the total it is built for). Cooking for 8 means doubling: 4 cups. Graphs work the same way. The bar height is the '2'; the title's units ('in hundreds') and the scale are the 'c.' and 'serves 4'. Read them first, then do the math the question needs.

blocks.text: Two tablespoons of flour instead of two cups ruins the cake. Eight visits instead of 800 ruins the answer.

explain.body: The title and axis labels tell you what is measured and in what unit. Words like 'in thousands' or '(%)' change what every value means.

test.q: A bar graph is titled 'Hospital meals served per day (in thousands)'. The bar for Tuesday reaches 2.5. How many meals were served on Tuesday?

whyNot.0: This moves the decimal one place, as if the unit were tens.
whyNot.1: This treats the unit as hundreds.
whyNot.3: This treats the unit as ten thousands.

explain.body: The legend matches each color or line style to a series. Describe a trend only across the points shown: rising, falling, steady or mixed.

test.q: A line graph's legend shows a solid line for yoga and a dashed line for spin. Sign-ups by month: yoga 10, 20, 30; spin 30, 25, 25. Which statement is supported?
options: Spin sign-ups rose each month
Yoga sign-ups rose each month
Spin led yoga in each of the 3 months
Yoga sign-ups stayed level after Month 2
test.why: Yoga went 10, 20, 30: an increase each month.

whyNot.0: Spin fell from 30 to 25, then stayed at 25.
whyNot.3: This describes the spin line, which stayed at 25.

explain.body: A pie chart gives shares of a whole. Count = percent × total. Without a total, you can compare slices but cannot give a number of people.

test.q: A pie chart shows the preferred contact method of 300 surveyed patients: text 50%, phone 30%, email 20%. How many patients prefer phone calls?

whyNot.0: 30 is the percentage, not the number of patients.
whyNot.1: 60 patients is the email slice (20% of 300).
whyNot.3: 150 patients is the text slice (50% of 300).

explain.body: In a flowchart, start at the top and answer each decision for the case given. On a map, real distance = map distance × scale; use the legend for symbols.

test.q: A state map's scale shows 1 inch = 30 miles. Two towns are 4 inches apart on the map. How far apart are they?
options: 7.5 miles
34 miles
90 miles
120 miles

whyNot.0: This divides 30 by 4 instead of multiplying.
whyNot.1: This adds 4 and 30 instead of multiplying.
whyNot.2: This multiplies by 3 inches instead of 4.
